title: All the way to the door
step: Level 3, rung 3 — the far side of the room
note:
Used three times. This is the walking one: mid-stride, going away, back mostly to the viewer. That motion is what tells it apart from door-stay-03-halfway, which is stopped and turned back.

The continuity:room reference to door-cover.png was removed before the first restyle round. Every rung carried both it and the continuity:ladder reference to the rung before, and their instructions contradict each other on the one thing the ladder cannot get wrong: the ladder role says match the previous rung's camera exactly, and the room role says match door-cover's camera exactly — but door-cover is a different shot, with the door open and the guest in it. Two attachments arguing about the camera is the shape of the round-1 failure. The previous rung is the room reference, and a better one: the tan-era record shows the camera holding to four pixels across four generations when each frame was attached to the last and nothing else competed. door-stay-03-onestep keeps its door-cover reference because it is the head of the ladder and has no previous rung to use instead.

Two sentences were removed from the scene text before the first restyle round because they contradicted the ladder rule stated three sentences above them in the same paragraph. 'Her back and shoulder mostly toward the viewer' is a rear three-quarter view, not the side-on one every other rung uses, and 'Lucy larger in frame than the handler' can only happen if the handler recedes into depth — both are camera moves, and the ladder's entire requirement is that the camera does not move. She is walking in profile now, which is what the fixed side view can actually show.

Worth knowing for whoever reviews this: the alt text in js/content.js says the handler 'stands at the closed front door', which is arrival rather than motion. The post-mortems, this spec and the near-duplicate test in scene.test.mjs all say walking, and walking is also what keeps this apart from door-stay-03-handle, which is the handler at the door with a hand on it. The alt text is the odd one out and has not been changed here.

Round 21 was approved and then found to have THREE hands: the two swinging arms plus a third hand with no arm, sitting just under the treat pouch where it read as part of the pouch and waistband. It survived a review because nothing on the sheet asks about anatomy — the six renditions ask about crops and sizes, and this is a full-size defect in the middle of the picture. A walking pose is where it is most likely: both arms are away from the body and the hip already carries a mustard object that a hand can be mistaken for.
scene: Interior entry hall, side view, camera at standing eye level. This is the same room, the same camera position and the same distance from the viewer as the other rungs of this ladder: Lucy's rectangular cool-grey dog bed on the left, the closed charcoal front door on the right, and a clear span of taupe-grey floor between them, with the whole walk from bed to door visible in frame. Lucy lies on the bed in a settled down — elbows and hips on the bed, head up and level, watching calmly. Her size in frame, the bed's position and the camera never change between these pictures. No leash. Only one thing changes from the previous rung: the handler has crossed the room and is arriving at the closed front door, and she is WALKING — caught mid-stride in the same side-on view as the other rungs, seen in profile moving to her right toward the door, with her leading foot forward and flat and the trailing heel clearly lifted off the floor. She faces the door and is not looking back at Lucy, and she is not stopped. Lucy lies on her bed at the left, holding her down and watching her go, drawn at exactly the same size and in exactly the same place as in the previous rung. The front door is still shut and no hand is on it yet. ANATOMY: she has exactly TWO arms and TWO hands, and no more. In this walking pose one arm swings forward and the other swings back, so both hands are visible — draw each one clearly joined to its own sleeve, and draw nothing that reads as a third hand anywhere in the picture, in particular not near the treat pouch at her hip, where a stray hand shape would sit against the pouch and the waistband and look deliberate.
mustBeTrue: the handler has exactly two arms and two hands, each hand joined to its own sleeve and no third hand anywhere near the pouch or waistband; she is unmistakably walking — one foot forward, the trailing heel lifted — moving away with her back toward the viewer and not looking round, while Lucy holds her down on the bed in the foreground and the door is still shut.
